title: Why the Florida Keys Hang on a Single Road
sources: Sea level: own calculation from NOAA CO-OPS monthly means, Key West 8724580 (geo/measure_sealevel.py)
People near US 1: own count from 2020 census blocks (US Census Bureau) and TIGER/Line roads (geo/measure_road.py)
Land height: own sample of 1,500 points, USGS 3DEP via EPQS (geo/measure_height.py)
Islands: 2020 census land blocks minus TIGER area water (geo/make_regions.py)
Road, railway, pipe, ferry, train and storm lines drawn through main points (approximate)

paragraphs.text: The Florida Keys hang on a single road. It runs more than a hundred miles out into the sea, farther than New York is from Philadelphia.
But it is the only road. Everything the islands need comes down it, even every drop of drinking water. And most of it sits only a few feet above the sea.

shots.photo: File:Seven Mile Bridge, Florida Keys aerial (2003).jpg

shots.on_screen_text: The Seven Mile Bridge from orbit

shots.photo: File:Overseas Highway to Key West - panoramio.jpg

paragraphs.text: So why would anyone build a highway across the sea, and can Florida keep it there?

shots.photo: File:The Lower Keys.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: The Lower Keys from the air

paragraphs.text: The road has already been lost once, to a storm that killed more than four hundred people. A city on it once declared that it had left the United States, because of a roadblock. And keeping the road out of the water now has a price that nobody wants to pay.

shots.photo: File:1935 hurricane effects in the Florida Keys MM00003786x (15479759252).jpg
shots.on_screen_text: The Keys after the storm of 1935

shots.photo: File:Key West 2008 (2338775214).jpg
File:001 Key West Bay Point - Lower Sugarloaf Channel aerial view.jpg

stat.label: To raise the county's roads above future tides

paragraphs.text: To see why, start at the far end of the road, with the town that made it worth building.
Reason one. At the end of the chain sat a town that was, for a while, the biggest in Florida.

shots.photo: File:Bird's eye view of Key West, Fla., Key West Island, C.S. Monroe Co., 1884 LOC 83693954.jpg

paragraphs.text: Key West has a deep, sheltered harbour on the Straits of Florida, the channel every ship takes between the Gulf of Mexico and the Atlantic. Cuba is about ninety miles away.

The town grew rich on that position. Ships wrecked on the reef offshore, and Key West salvaged them, under a federal court that sat in the town to divide the cargo. Later it rolled cigars with tobacco from Cuba, and the Navy kept a base there.

shots.photo: File:The Harbor House, Front Street, Key West, Florida.jpg
File:1909 hurricane effects in Key West MM00000841x (15413985922).jpg
File:Old Post Office and Customshouse, Key West.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: The old federal building, Key West

shots.photo: File:Key West Florida - Ann Street - Cortez Cigar Factory.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: A cigar factory on Ann Street

shots.photo: File:Aerial view of Naval Air Station Key West - Boca Chica Field in April 2016.JPG
shots.on_screen_text: Naval Air Station Key West today

paragraphs.text: In the census of 1890, Key West had about eighteen thousand people. That was more than Jacksonville, and more than any other city in Florida.

shots.photo: File:Pohalski City Key West Florida 1889.jpg

paragraphs.text: It was a town that kept losing its trades. Lighthouses made the reef safer, so fewer ships wrecked. Then most of the cigar makers moved to Tampa, on the mainland.

shots.photo: File:Key West Florida Sponge Wagon 1930s.jpg
File:Key West Lighthouse 20080728.jpg

paragraphs.text: But it had no road to the rest of the country. Everything came and went by ship.
In 1905 the United States began to dig the Panama Canal. Key West was the closest deep-water American port to it.

A railroad owner named Henry Flagler saw a bet. His Florida East Coast Railway already ran down the coast to Miami and Homestead. If he could carry his tracks to Key West, the trade of the canal and of Cuba could come by rail.

shots.photo: File:Opening of Florida Keys Railway - J.R. Parott, H. M. Flagler LCCN2014680212.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Henry Flagler and his railway men, 1912

paragraphs.text: The problem was the hundred and twenty-eight miles in between. Most of it was water.

stat.label: Homestead to Key West by the railway's route

paragraphs.text: The road we drive today started as his railroad. And the railroad was a far harder thing to build.

shots.photo: File:Long Key Viaduct, view showing typical method of construction for all concrete arches in 7-Mile Bridge (-214). - Seven Mile Bridge, Linking Florida Keys, Marathon, Monroe County HAER FLA,44-KNIKE,1-52.tif
File:Knight's Key Bridge, view of derrick lowering cofferdam (Lindenberg Collection -1569). - Seven Mile Bridge, Linking Florida Keys, Marathon, Monroe County, FL HAER FLA,44-KNIKE,1-53.tif

paragraphs.text: Reason two. Before there was a road, there was a railroad across the sea.

shots.photo: File:A guide to Florida for tourists, sportsmen and settlers (1912) (14576579758).jpg
shots.on_screen_text: The line over the sea, 1912 guidebook

paragraphs.text: Work began in 1905. Thousands of men cleared mangroves, dredged fill out of the shallows, and poured concrete into the water.

shots.photo: File:Knight's Key Bridge, view of first span, 1909 (-2518). - Seven Mile Bridge, Linking Florida Keys, Marathon, Monroe County, FL HAER FLA,44-KNIKE,1-51.tif
shots.on_screen_text: The first span at Knight's Key, 1909

shots.photo: File:Knight's Key Bridge, View of steel girders in place and on barge (-571). - Seven Mile Bridge, Linking Florida Keys, Marathon, Monroe County, FL HAER FLA,44-KNIKE,1-44.tif

paragraphs.text: The surveyors barely knew the islands. Halfway down Key Largo they found a lake no map had shown. The fill kept sinking into its soft bottom, and they named it Lake Surprise.

shots.on_screen_text: Lake Surprise, with US 1 across it

paragraphs.text: Then came the storms. In October 1906 a hurricane tore a floating barracks loose from its moorings, and about a hundred workers died. More hurricanes hit in 1909 and 1910.

stat.label: A hurricane tears loose a floating workers' barracks

shots.photo: File:1910 hurricane effects in Key West MM00011137x (26387467093).jpg
File:1909 hurricane effects in Key West MM00000841x (15413985922).jpg

paragraphs.text: Where the gaps were short, the crews built long rows of concrete arches. The Long Key Viaduct ran for about two miles just above the sea, and the railway put it on its posters.

shots.on_screen_text: The Long Key Viaduct's arches today

shots.photo: File:Knight's Key Bridge, passenger train crossing bridge, no date (Bramson Collection, X-336-1). - Seven Mile Bridge, Linking Florida Keys, Marathon, Monroe County, FL HAER FLA,44-KNIKE,1-72.tif
shots.on_screen_text: A passenger train on the Knight's Key bridge

paragraphs.text: Where the water was deepest, at Bahia Honda, they built a steel truss bridge. West of Marathon came the longest gap of all, crossed by the Seven Mile Bridge. Its builders lived under it, on a five-acre island called Pigeon Key.

shots.photo: File:Knight's Key Bridge, long side perspective, 12-22-26 (Matlack 141-40). - Seven Mile Bridge, Linking Florida Keys, Marathon, Monroe County, FL HAER FLA,44-KNIKE,1-59.tif

paragraphs.text: Even Key West itself was too small for the railway. There was no room on the island for a big rail yard and docks, so a dredging company pumped up the shallows and built about a hundred and thirty acres of new land, at Trumbo Point.

shots.photo: File:Aerial photo of Trumbo Point Annex of Naval Air Station Key West in April 2016.JPG

paragraphs.text: The work never stopped for long. Men came and went by the thousand, because few stayed more than a season in the heat, the mosquitoes and the storms.

shots.photo: File:Long Key Viaduct, view showing typical method of construction for all concrete arches in 7-Mile Bridge (-214). - Seven Mile Bridge, Linking Florida Keys, Marathon, Monroe County HAER FLA,44-KNIKE,1-52.tif

paragraphs.text: On the twenty-second of January 1912, the first train rolled into Key West. Flagler was on board. He was eighty-two years old, and he died the next year.

stat.label: The first train arrives in Key West

shots.photo: File:Opening of Florida Keys Railway - J.R. Parott, H. M. Flagler LCCN2014680212.jpg

shots.on_screen_text: Trumbo Point, the end of the line

paragraphs.text: From 1915, ferries carried whole freight cars from Key West to Havana, so a wagon loaded in New York could be unloaded in Cuba.
Then the business did not come. The canal opened in 1914, but the ships kept going where they had always gone. Freight on the single track stayed thin.

stat.label: The Panama Canal opens

paragraphs.text: Cars came too. In 1928 a road opened down the upper islands, but it stopped at Lower Matecumbe Key. From there, cars went on a ferry for about forty miles, a trip of around four hours, to the next stretch of road at No Name Key.

shots.photo: File:Photograph of a road sign along the highway in Key West, Florida, announcing the beginning of U.S. Route 1 to Fort... - NARA - 200542.jpg

paragraphs.text: So for a few years, the Keys had two half-links to the mainland. Then the sea decided which one would stay.
Reason three. The road exists because the sea destroyed the railroad.

shots.photo: File:Labor Day hurricane weather map (enlarged), September 1, 1935 (4399800).jpg

paragraphs.text: By then Key West was in deep trouble. The Navy had closed its base, and in the Depression most of the town lived on relief. In July 1934 the city gave up and handed its powers to the state. Federal relief officials took over, and they decided Key West's future was tourists. The tourists would need a road.

shots.photo: File:Key West Florida Sponge Wagon 1930s.jpg

stat.label: Share of Key West on relief, 1934
Key West hands its powers to the state

shots.photo: File:Florida - Key West - NARA - 23936667.jpg
File:Old Post Office and Customshouse, Key West.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Old Post Office and Customs House, Key West

paragraphs.text: In 1934, the federal government sent hundreds of out-of-work veterans of the First World War to the Keys. They lived in camps of wooden huts and built bridges to close the ferry gap.

shots.photo: File:Veterans Storm Relief Map.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Veterans' camps and the storm, 1936 relief map

paragraphs.text: On Labor Day, the second of September 1935, a small hurricane crossed the Keys near Long Key. Its central pressure was 892 millibars. No storm on record has come ashore in the United States with lower pressure.

stat.label: Lowest pressure of any US landfall on record

shots.on_screen_text: Long Key, where the eye crossed

paragraphs.text: Its winds are now estimated at about a hundred and eighty-five miles an hour. The sea rose over the islands with it.

stat.label: Estimated one-minute winds

shots.photo: File:1935 Labor Day hurricane path.png

paragraphs.text: A train was sent from Miami to bring the veterans out. It was held at a drawbridge over the Miami River and reached Islamorada late, just as the surge did.
The water swept every car off the track. Only the locomotive stayed on the rails. Everyone on the train lived, but the camps were gone.

shots.photo: File:1935 hurricane effects in the Florida Keys MM00003786x (15479759252).jpg

paragraphs.text: The official count is 408 dead, and later counts went higher. More than half of them were veterans. About half of the men in the camps were away in Miami that weekend, or the toll would have been worse.

stat.label: Official count of the dead

shots.photo: File:Burial of 1935 hurricane victims at Woodlawn Cemetery, Miami, FL.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Burial of storm victims, Miami, September 1935

stat.label: Camp veterans away in Miami that weekend

paragraphs.text: The storm washed away about forty miles of track. The railway was already bankrupt, and it did not rebuild.

shots.photo: File:Labor Day hurricane weather map, September 4, 1935 (high quality) (3099770).jpg

paragraphs.text: In 1936 the state of Florida bought the whole right-of-way, with its bridges, for six hundred and forty thousand dollars.

shots.photo: File:Knight's Key Bridge, long side perspective, 12-22-26 (Matlack 141-40). - Seven Mile Bridge, Linking Florida Keys, Marathon, Monroe County, FL HAER FLA,44-KNIKE,1-59.tif

stat.label: Price of the railway right-of-way and bridges, 1936
stat.source: Keys historian J. Wilkinson; Fla. Supreme Court 1936

paragraphs.text: Then it laid a road on top. Concrete decks went over the old railway bridges. In 1938 the Overseas Highway opened, and for the first time you could drive to Key West.

shots.photo: File:Pigeon Key Bridge, aerial view w-auto traffic, April 23, 1938 (Matlack 397-13-7). - Seven Mile Bridge, Linking Florida Keys, Marathon, Monroe County, FL HAER FLA,44-KNIKE,1-66.tif
shots.on_screen_text: Cars on the new highway, April 1938

paragraphs.text: At Bahia Honda, the steel truss was too narrow for two lanes of cars. So the road was laid across the top of it, sixty-five feet above the water.

shots.photo: File:Bahia Honda Bridge, highest span of Overseas Highway on way to Key West, Florida.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: The Bahia Honda bridge, road on top

shots.photo: File:FDR in an open car by the Bahia Honda Bridge on February 19, 1939 (8150911081).jpg
shots.on_screen_text: President Roosevelt at the Bahia Honda bridge, 1939

shots.photo: File:Bahia Honda Rail Bridge(js).jpg

paragraphs.text: Two weeks after the storm, the writer Ernest Hemingway, who lived in Key West, published an article about the camps. Its title was a question: who murdered the vets? He blamed Washington for leaving the men on low islands in the hurricane season.

shots.photo: File:Hemingwayhouse.jpg

stat.label: Hemingway: "Who Murdered the Vets?"

shots.on_screen_text: The low islands of the Matecumbe Keys

paragraphs.text: Today a stone memorial stands at Islamorada. The remains of some of the dead are inside it.

shots.photo: File:Veterans Storm Relief Map.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: The 1936 relief map of the storm

paragraphs.text: So the road won. But the road had a problem the railroad never solved. The islands it joined had nothing to drink.

shots.photo: File:Baihia Honda Bridge - Flickr - daniel.chodusov.jpg

paragraphs.text: Reason four. The Keys cannot live without the mainland, because they have no fresh water of their own.

shots.photo: File:Fkeast 2000.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: The Upper Keys, NOAA sanctuary map

paragraphs.text: The upper islands are the top of an old coral reef. The rock is full of holes. Rain sinks straight through it and mixes with the sea.

shots.photo: File:Fossil Reef Windley Key 1.jpg

paragraphs.text: So for more than a century, Key West drank rain. Every house caught water from its roof in a cistern.

shots.photo: File:Pink and Blue House in Key West, Florida.jpg
File:CISTERNS AT REAR, LOOKING SOUTHEAST - Tift and Company, Ships Chandlery and Icehouse, Mallory Square, Key West, Monroe County, FL HABS FLA,44-KEY,8-3.tif
shots.on_screen_text: Cisterns behind a Key West warehouse

paragraphs.text: That worked for a town. It did not work for a naval base during a war.

shots.photo: File:3-4 VIEW TO NORTHEAST - Naval Air Station Key West, Truman Annex, Fresh Water Cistern, Intersection of Front and Eaton Streets, Key West, Monroe County, FL HABS fl-530-C-4.tif
shots.on_screen_text: A Navy fresh-water cistern, Key West

shots.photo: File:Sally Rand Visits Key West Naval Hospital.jpg

paragraphs.text: In 1941 the Navy bought land at Florida City on the mainland for wells. It laid a pipe down the old railroad route, island by island, about a hundred and thirty miles.
On the twenty-second of September 1942, fresh water from the mainland reached Key West for the first time. It took about six days to get there.

stat.label: Mainland water reaches Key West for the first time

shots.photo: File:Florida - Key West - NARA - 23936663.jpg

paragraphs.text: That pipe changed what the Keys could be. With water you could build hotels, and fill pools, and live there all year. In 1940, about fourteen thousand people lived in the county. Twenty years later, nearly forty-eight thousand did.

shots.photo: File:Florida - Key West - NARA - 23936671.jpg
File:Sunset Key and Sailboats, Florida, 2025.jpg
File:“Welcome to Marathon,” Marathon, Florida Keys.jpg

paragraphs.text: Today the water still comes from the wellfield at Florida City. It runs down the chain in a big pipe beside the highway, across the same bridges, all the way to Key West.

shots.on_screen_text: Florida City, where the wells are
The pipe crosses on the bridges

paragraphs.text: The pipe still carries about seventeen million gallons a day. The whole system now has more than a thousand miles of pipe.

stat.label: Gallons of water a day down the pipe

shots.photo: File:7 Mile Bridge www.florida-infos.com - panoramio (1).jpg

paragraphs.text: The power comes down the chain in the same way. So does the fuel, and almost all the food.

shots.photo: File:Key West 2008 (2338775214).jpg

paragraphs.text: And the people live along it too. We took every block of the 2020 census in the Keys and measured how far it lies from US 1.
Half of all the people in the Keys live within a quarter of a mile of the highway. More than nine in ten live within a mile of it.

stat.label: Keys residents within a quarter mile of US 1
stat.source: Own count: 2020 census blocks vs US 1 (geo/measure_road.py)

stat.label: Keys residents within one mile of US 1
stat.source: Own count: 2020 census blocks vs US 1 (geo/measure_road.py)

paragraphs.text: There is a backup. Two plants in the Keys can turn seawater into drinking water, and they are kept for the days when the pipe is cut. After Irma, they were switched on. The newer one, opened in 2025, makes about four million gallons a day, roughly a quarter of what the islands use.

shots.photo: File:Debris (36884162550).jpg

stat.label: Gallons a day from the Stock Island seawater plant (2025)

paragraphs.text: Everything the islands need comes in through one narrow strip. And a strip that narrow can be closed.

shots.on_screen_text: Where the road leaves the mainland

shots.photo: File:Overseas Highway to Key West - panoramio.jpg

paragraphs.text: Reason five. A chain of islands with one road has one door. In 1982, somebody shut it.

Two years earlier, more than a hundred and twenty-five thousand Cubans had crossed the Straits in small boats. Most of them landed at Key West. On one day in May 1980, more than four and a half thousand arrived. The Border Patrol now watched the one road out.

stat.label: Cubans in the Mariel boatlift, 1980

shots.photo: File:Mariel Boatlift refugee center (7164017325).jpg

stat.label: Cubans arriving at Key West on 11 May 1980

paragraphs.text: In April 1982, the Border Patrol set up a roadblock on the highway just south of Florida City. Every car leaving the Keys was stopped and searched.

shots.photo: File:The Lower Keys.jpg

paragraphs.text: The queue ran for miles. Tourists stayed away. Key West's leaders went to a federal court, and the court refused to stop it.

shots.photo: File:Key West City Hall.jpg

paragraphs.text: So on the twenty-third of April, the mayor of Key West read out a proclamation. The city had left the United States, he said, and was now the Conch Republic.

stat.label: Key West declares itself the Conch Republic

shots.photo: File:The Conch Republic Flag, Key West, Florida, June 2021.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: The Conch Republic flag, Key West

paragraphs.text: It was a joke, and everyone knew it. But the roadblock came down soon after, and the Keys still celebrate the day.

shots.photo: File:Mallory Square, Key West - panoramio (5).jpg
File:Key West Florida 2014 - Conch Republic Passport Office.jpg

paragraphs.text: The joke was about a real thing. The same road that lets people in is the only way out. And in a hurricane, everyone has to use it at once.

shots.on_screen_text: One road in, one road out

paragraphs.text: So Florida law sets a limit. All the permanent residents of the Keys must be able to drive out to the mainland in no more than twenty-four and a half hours.

stat.label: Legal limit to evacuate the Keys' permanent residents

paragraphs.text: Until 2025, the limit was twenty-four hours. The state added half an hour, and ordered a new count of how many more homes that would allow.

stat.label: Hours allowed, before and after the 2025 law

paragraphs.text: That limit decides how many new homes may be built. More houses mean more cars on one road, so the state hands out building permits in small numbers each year.
The rule has a hard edge. People in mobile homes do not count as permanent residents, because they are ordered out first, before everyone else.

shots.photo: File:Debris (36884162550).jpg

paragraphs.text: In September 2017, the door was tested. Hurricane Irma was heading for the Keys. On the morning of the sixth of September, all visitors were ordered to leave. That evening, the order went out to every resident.

shots.photo: File:Irma 2017-09-10 1315Z.jpg

stat.label: Visitors ordered out at 7 a.m., residents at 7 p.m.

paragraphs.text: On the tenth of September it came ashore at Cudjoe Key, in the Lower Keys, as a category four storm.
Nearly twelve hundred homes were destroyed. Most of them were mobile homes and small, older houses.

stat.label: Homes destroyed by Irma in the Keys

shots.photo: File:Hurricane Irma 19 (36977734710).jpg

paragraphs.text: Before anyone could go back, engineers had to inspect all forty-two bridges. Two short stretches of the highway had washed out near Marathon and had to be rebuilt first.

shots.on_screen_text: Officials in the Keys after Irma

paragraphs.text: The road came back within days. But the homes that blew away were the cheapest in the Keys, and with permits capped, many of them never came back.

shots.photo: File:Florida night-time satellite image before-and-after Hurricane Irma.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Florida's lights before and after Irma

paragraphs.text: The door has held, so far. But the threat to it now is not one storm. It is the sea itself.

chapters.title: The Sea Is Coming Up the Road

paragraphs.text: Reason six. The road was built at the level of the sea in 1938. The sea is no longer there.

shots.photo: File:Pigeon Key Bridge, aerial view w-auto traffic, April 23, 1938 (Matlack 397-13-7). - Seven Mile Bridge, Linking Florida Keys, Marathon, Monroe County, FL HAER FLA,44-KNIKE,1-66.tif

paragraphs.text: How low is the land? We took fifteen hundred random points on the land of the Keys, mangrove islands included, and looked up the height of each one in the federal elevation survey.

shots.on_screen_text: Mangrove islands of the Lower Keys

paragraphs.text: Four-fifths of the land stands less than three feet above the sea. Nine-tenths is under five feet. The highest ground is only about twenty feet up.

chart.title: Share of the Keys' land
chart.source: Own sample: 1,500 land points, USGS 3DEP elevations (geo/measure_height.py)

paragraphs.text: Key West has measured the sea since 1913, one of the longest tide records in the country. We took NOAA's monthly readings and averaged them.
The sea at Key West is now about a foot higher than when the gauge began. And over the last thirty years it has risen more than twice as fast as the century before.

chart.title: Sea level at Key West vs 1913-22
chart.source: Own calculation: NOAA monthly mean sea level, Key West, 1913-2025 (geo/measure_sealevel.py)

stat.label: Rise since 1996 vs the 1913-2025 rate (6.4 vs 2.65 mm a year)
stat.source: Own calculation: NOAA monthly mean sea level, Key West, 1913-2025 (geo/measure_sealevel.py)

paragraphs.text: On the islands that shows up as water in the streets, on days with no storm at all. In the autumn of 2019, the streets of one Key Largo neighbourhood, Stillwright Point, stayed under the tide for ninety-four days in a row.

shots.photo: File:Pink and Blue House in Key West, Florida.jpg

stat.label: Streets under the king tides, autumn 2019

paragraphs.text: The county has worked out what it would take to raise its own roads, about a hundred and fifty miles of them, above the tides to come. The answer was about one point eight billion dollars.

stat.label: To raise about 150 miles of county roads

paragraphs.text: The first neighbourhood is being rebuilt now, at Twin Lakes in Key Largo. Less than a mile of road, with pumps and drains, for about twenty-two million dollars.

stat.label: Twin Lakes road project, under one mile

paragraphs.text: The state has rebuilt the highway before. In the early 1980s it replaced thirty-seven of the forty-four old bridges, most of them Flagler's railway spans with a road on top. The new Seven Mile Bridge opened in 1982.

shots.photo: File:7 Mile Bridge www.florida-infos.com - panoramio (1).jpg

stat.label: Old bridges replaced in the early 1980s

shots.photo: File:Knight's Key Bridge, passenger train crossing bridge, no date (Bramson Collection, X-336-1). - Seven Mile Bridge, Linking Florida Keys, Marathon, Monroe County, FL HAER FLA,44-KNIKE,1-72.tif

shots.on_screen_text: The new and old Seven Mile Bridges

paragraphs.text: And that is only the side streets. The highway belongs to the state. Its longest bridge, the Seven Mile Bridge of 1982, is likely to be replaced, and the state's early estimate for a new one is about six hundred and seventy-seven million dollars.

shots.photo: File:Seven Mile Bridge, Florida Keys aerial (2003).jpg

stat.label: Early estimate for a new Seven Mile Bridge

paragraphs.text: Even the reason most visitors come is changing. In the summer of 2023 the sea around the Keys grew hotter than it had been in any record, and nearly all the remaining elkhorn and staghorn coral on the reef died. Scientists now call both species functionally extinct there.

shots.photo: File:Elkhorn coral 8 Molasses Reef 20080309.jpg

stat.label: Hottest water on Florida's reef in the record
Of the remaining elkhorn and staghorn corals died, 2023
Elkhorn and staghorn coral in Florida after 2023

paragraphs.text: About eighty thousand people live in the Keys. Every road raised and every bridge replaced is paid for by them, by the state, and often by federal grants.

stat.label: People in the Keys

paragraphs.text: The old Seven Mile Bridge is still there, beside the new one. Its first two miles are a footpath now, out to Pigeon Key. Further on, a span is missing, where the boats pass through.

shots.photo: File:Fred the Tree 2025-05-18.jpg
File:Christmastime Fred the Tree.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: The old bridge, now a footpath

shots.photo: File:Baihia Honda Bridge - Flickr - daniel.chodusov.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: A missing span: the old Bahia Honda bridge

paragraphs.text: So this is why the Florida Keys hang on a single road.

A town at the end of the chain was worth reaching. A railroad reached it, and the storm of 1935 took the railroad and left the road. The islands had no water, so the water came down the road too. And because it is the only road, it is also the only way out, the reason the Keys are allowed to grow so little.

shots.photo: File:Bird's eye view of Key West, Fla., Key West Island, C.S. Monroe Co., 1884 LOC 83693954.jpg
File:A guide to Florida for tourists, sportsmen and settlers (1912) (14576579758).jpg
File:3-4 VIEW TO NORTHEAST - Naval Air Station Key West, Truman Annex, Fresh Water Cistern, Intersection of Front and Eaton Streets, Key West, Monroe County, FL HABS fl-530-C-4.tif
File:Sunset Key and Sailboats, Florida, 2025.jpg

paragraphs.text: The roadblock of 1982 showed what one door means. The storm of 1935 showed what the sea can take. The price of keeping the road is the open question.

shots.photo: File:The Conch Republic Flag, Key West, Florida, June 2021.jpg
File:1935 Labor Day hurricane path.png

paragraphs.text: The numbers we measured say how tight the bet is. Nine in ten people live within a mile of one road. Four-fifths of the land stands less than three feet above the sea. And that sea is about a foot higher than it was when the gauge at Key West began.

stat.label: Within one mile of US 1
stat.source: Own count: 2020 census blocks vs US 1 (geo/measure_road.py)

stat.label: Of the land under 3 feet
stat.source: Own sample: 1,500 land points, USGS 3DEP elevations (geo/measure_height.py)

stat.label: Sea level at Key West since the gauge began
stat.source: Own calculation: NOAA monthly mean sea level, Key West, 1913-2025 (geo/measure_sealevel.py)

paragraphs.text: Florida has rebuilt this road twice already, once from a railroad and once with new bridges. The next rebuild will have to lift it.

shots.photo: File:Bahia Honda Rail Bridge(js).jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Old and new bridges at Bahia Honda

paragraphs.text: Would you keep paying to hold a road above a rising sea, or should the Keys one day go back to boats?

shots.photo: File:001 Key West Bay Point - Lower Sugarloaf Channel aerial view.jpg

ask.text: Keep paying to hold the road above the sea, or go back to boats?

Why America Built a Highway Across the Sea
Why the Florida Keys Have Only One Way Out
youtube.description: The Florida Keys hang on one road, more than a hundred miles of highway and bridges over the sea. Their people, their drinking water and their only way out all depend on it. We follow why it was built and whether it can be kept: Key West, once the biggest city in Florida; Flagler's railroad across the sea; the Labor Day hurricane of 1935 that destroyed it and left the road; the 1942 Navy pipe that still carries every drop of water; the 1982 roadblock and the Conch Republic; the 24.5-hour evacuation rule that caps new homes; Hurricane Irma; and the rising sea, measured at the Key West tide gauge since 1913.
youtube.pinned_comment: Would you keep paying to hold a road above a rising sea, or should the Keys one day go back to boats?
